Bibliamar Stefanson, der frucht-
bare amerikanische Neutrality-suspicious.
ist überzeugt, daß der hohe Norden
bewohnbar ist und reich kommt von
der freundlichen Arktis. Dieser in
Kanada geborene, von isländis-
chen Eltern stammende Celebrat hat seit
Beginn des Sabrumberts die Geoden
der nördlichen Polarregion wissen-
schaftlich erforscht und eine spielen-
denschaftliche Bibliothek von Spitzberg-
en Inseln und gegen jeden anderen
Breitengrad zusammengetragen, in der
die diese grenzlose Deutung unersetz-
lich ist. Das Amt für Warineforschung
der US. Staaten hat ihn deshalbe be-
auftragt, eine Wissenschaft der Arktis
im Umfang von fünf Millionen
Worten zusammenzustellen. Zehn
Wissenschaftler arbeiten unter Stefanson-
s Leitung schon seit Monaten daran,
und im Jahre 1950 oder 1961
soll das Werk in einem kommerziellen
Verlag erscheinen. Es werden darin
die Gebiete behandelt sein, die immer
bald des Polarfreihes liegen, also auch
die zu Grönland geborenen Gegenden,
die in der letzten Zeit stark kolonisiert
wurden.

Der Forscher widmet auch der Arktis-
ischen Bedeutung der nördlichen
Polargebiete große Aufmerksamkeit.
Er meint darauf hin, daß nicht nur in
Nord-Amerika Bemühungen zur Ge-
neralization der Lebens- und Industrie-
zentren im Gange sind, sondern
noch viel mehr in Grönland. Er stellt
fest, daß die Amerikaner
ihren Pioniergeist verloren,
der ihre Vorfahren vor hundert Jahr-
en durch den Sentiment trieb.
Durch den gewaltigen Fortschritt der
Schifffahrt und der dadurch begünstigten
Transporterleistungen würden In-
tresionen auf die Besiedlung
Alaska, Kanadas und Labrador's
angehen, sondern die Bevölkerung kann
sie sich in den Gebieten mit adanya-
nem Glanz, wie etwa Süd-Kaliforn-
ien, vorstellen. Er fordert die amerikanische
Gesellschaft auf, den Grönland-Aus-
bau in der Erschließung der Arktis
durch Gründung einer Kolonisations-
gesellschaft mitzunehmen, und teilt
als Beispiel auf die große Spitze
hin, daß die US-Besiedlung der
Glacier-Region in Grönland die
selbe Methode anwendet von den rus-
sischen Intrusionen. Er berichtet
folgendes Bild:

Im hohen Norden gibt es so viele
kleine Städte mit 10000 bis 40,-
600 Einwohnern wie amerikanische
und kanadische Dörfer mit drei oder
vierhundert. Zur Ausbeutung der
Rohstoffvorkommen im Labrador-Raum,
das rund einhundertsechsundsiebzig Kilometer
nördlich des Polarfreihes und drei-
hundertachtzig Kilometer östlich von
Wurmänif liegt, errichteten die Minen-
le die Stadt Bourtuta, die nun 80
600 Einwohner hat. Sie hatten eine
Bahnlinie von rund tausend Kilometer
lange, legten Stahl Schienen über Pro-
BUTTON von Gemini und Meiß an und
erreichten nach gründlichen Bemühungen,
doch während des kurzen, aber warmen
Sommers der arktischen Nordzone,
Rentier und Kartoffeln hervorbrachten.
Bourtuta ist nun, nach Stefanson's an-
geben, das fünftgrößte Rohstoff-
zentrum der Spitzbergen-Union,
das die Kontinenten von Grönland
beherrscht.

MOSCOW, Feb. 26,—The American Embassy is making extensive inquiries about Angus Ward, its consul general at Mukden, China. He last was in touch with the State Department November 15.

Mr. Ward had 10 members of the consulate staff with him when his link with the United States was severed by the entrance of Chinese Communist troops.

The Embassy here has had no success.

for new trial thwarted. Thomas
A. Edwards today prepared to face
sentence for the murder OF John
H. Mahlan. 25-year-old Glen
Burnie postal clerk and his COM
panion. Miss Mary c. Kline, Is.


The defendants prospects of
sentence were narrowly circum-
scribed by law: Either death on
the gallows or life Imprisonment.
An appeal. Of course, may be
taken.


Edwards attorneys. William j.
McWilliams and Ridgely p. Mel
win. asked for a retrial on the
basis of new evidence they said
they had uncovered. And they
claimed the 24-year-old colored
man had been "framed''-not by
police. but by someone else"


New Trial Refused.


But yesterday six of seven
judges on the supreme bench of
Baltimore overruled the motion
for new trial. Judge Michael J.
Manley withheld his signature.
No opinions or comments were
given.


Edwards was convicted of first
degree murder last February. No
date for his sentence has been set,
but court attaches expect it with
In a week or so.


The husky sugar refinery work.
er's confession to police that he
shot the young Glen Burnie pair
last September was attacked by his
counsel. Prosecutors argued that
Edwards was cunning. cruel, de-
ceptive" and that nothing could
have induced him to sign an ad-
mission against his will. =


The principal arguments with
which the defense supported it's
plea for retrial were that the
Chesterfield road clearing where
the bodies were found was known
to Miss Kline and her escort and
that an empty cartridge shell
found at that lonely spot strange
ly did not turn up in a thorough
police search the day the bodies
were found.


Found Six Days Later.


That shell. the only one def
nitely linked to Edwards gun, was
found by O curiosity seeker six
days later.


The State had claimed and the
written confession supported this.
that Edwards drove the two to the
Chesterfield clearing and that the
killing Of Mahlan took place near
Glen Burnie.


Mr.. McWilliams contended Sat-
urday. when arguments were
heard. that 1t was impossible TO
swallow the statement" that Ed
wards by coincidence took them to
the clearing which on the basis
of the new evidence" must be
supposed familiar to the pair.


He drew this conclusion from
statements the defense attributed
to Miss Margaret Armstrong, a
friend of Miss Kline's. who now
lives at the YWCA in Alexandria.

work of fiction Mr.. O'Hara has
changed to Fort Penn. Most OF
the events take place between
1903 and 1920.


There are many characters, but
the story is centered around Grace
Caldwell Tate, daughter of the
William Penn Caldwells. the most
influential and one of the Wealth.
est families in Fort Penn. 1t is
primarily the chronicle of her
marriage to Sidney Tate, a young
New Yorker, who also has ample
means. The Tates settle on the
nearby Caldwell farm, because
they both love the country, and
there they bring up their three
children and do some genteel
farming and a lot of entertaining.


The story of the Tates Is told
against a panoramic background
of the town and its people. The
whole complex structure Of Fort
Penn Is explored-State and local
politics, more especially the city
machine; the social life Of the
elite; the intrigues and jealousies,
friendships and hatreds that color
the history of any city.


A Broken Ideal.


Grace and Sidney Tate seem an
ideal couple until a time in the
spring of 1917. after they've been
married IA years. The husband
discovers that his wife has been
carrying on an affair with Roger
Bannon, the wild son of ward
politician. Tragedy follows the
family for a while, not all Of 1t
resulting from the Bannon inter-
lude. It is a critical period.
Grace faces another in 1920, when
her story reaches a climax.


These two crescendos in the
slow narrative of her life crash
with dramatic impact. Unfortu-
nately much of the book moves at
a pedestrian pace through multi
tude of detail which often is ir-
relevant. "a Rage to Live" is not
so much a novel as transcript in
which an omniscient narrator
seems to have recorded everything
that every incidental person said,
felt and did. Consequently the
book seems even longer than its
$50 pages. There are whole pages
in which the assessed valuation of
Fort Penn properties and the
trends of business are discussed
solemnly. People exchange the
amenities at length. All this may
be realism, but it suggests Dresser
at his most verbose.


Unbridled Sex.


When 1t comes to the sex life
of his characters, Mr.. O'Hara is
even less reticent. Nothing is i'm
piled, all is described. There is
never, in this or other details, that
subtlety of suggestion. that power
to touch the readers imagination
with a hint and a glimpse, which
is the essence of literary art.


Sidney Tate was the only char
acter I could admire. II is hard
to feel sympathy for Grace. not
because she gives way OCCASION
ally to what she calls uncontrolla-
BILE impulses. but because she
is so dull. SShe takes advice
from stupid people and discusses
her most intimate problems with
Just any one, including a servant.
She puts up with a busybody
friend named Connie, who turns
out to be a lesbian. There
seems to be no such thing as a
secret or even a private life in
Fort Penn. 1t Is doubtful if pru-
rience ever got into print in
grosser detail than on these pages.


BY sheer weight of words, "a
Rage to Live" attains viv;dness.
It's people are clear enough. But
I cannot see that this novel adds
anything to American literature.

1903 and 1920.


There are many characters, but
the story is centered around Grace
Caldwell Tate, daughter of the
William Penn Caldwells, the most
influential and one of the wealthiest
families in Fort Penn. It is
primarily the chronicle of her
marriage to Sidney Tate, a young
New Yorker, who also has ample
means. The Tates settle on the
nearby Caldwell farm, because
they both love the country, and
there they bring up their three
children and do some genteel
farming and a lot of entertaining.


The story of the Tates is told
against a panoramic background
of the town and its people. The
whole complex structure of Fort
Penn is explored—State and local
politics, more especially the city
machine; the social life of the
elite; the intrigues and jealousies,
friendships and hatreds that color
the history of any city.


A Broken Ideal.


Grace and Sidney Tate seem an
ideal couple until a time in the
spring of 1917, after they've been
married 14 years. The husband
discovers that his wife has been
carrying on an affair with Roger
Bannon, the wild son of a ward
politician. Tragedy follows the
family for a while, not all of it
resulting from the Bannon inter-
lude. It is a critical period.
Grace faces another in 1920, when
her story reaches a climax.


These two crescendos in the
slow narrative of her life crash
with dramatic impact. Unfortu-
nately much of the book moves at
a pedestrian pace through multi-
tude of detail which often is ir-
relevant. "A Rage to Live" is not
so much a novel as a transcript in
which an omniscient narrator
seems to have recorded everything
that every incidental person said,
felt and did. Consequently the
book seems even longer than its
550 pages. There are whole pages
in which the assessed valuation of
Fort Penn properties and the
trends of business are discussed
solemnly. People exchange the
amenities at length. All this may
be realism, but it suggests Dresser
at his most verbose.


Unbridled Sex.


When it comes to the sex life
of his characters, Mr. O'Hara is
even less reticent. Nothing is im-
plied, all is described. There is
never, in this or other details, that
subtlety of suggestion, that power
to touch the reader's imagination
with a hint and a glimpse, which
is the essence of literary art.


Sidney Tate was the only char-
acter I could admire. It is hard
to feel sympathy for Grace, not
because she gives way occasionally
to what she calls uncontrolla-
ble impulses, but because she
is so dull. She takes advice
from stupid people and discusses
her most intimate problems with
just anyone, including a servant.
She puts up with a busybody
friend named Connie, who turns
out to be a lesbian. There
seems to be no such thing as a
secret or even a private life in
Fort Penn. It is doubtful if pru-
dence ever got into print in
grosser detail than on these pages.


By sheer weight of words, "A
Rage to Live" attains vividness.
Its people are clear enough. But
I cannot see that this novel adds
anything to American literature.

NEW YORK (P)—Federal Judge Sylvester J. Ryan ruled today that Judith Coplon must stand trial with Russian engineer Vanentine Gubitchev on spy conspiracy charges.

Ryan denied a motion by the ex-government girl's lawyer, Archibald Palmer, to hold that the trial would put his client in double jeopardy—that is, put her on trial twice for the same offense.

Miss Coplon already has been convicted in Washington on similar charge involving the theft of official secrets for passing on to the Russians.

The judge directed that she and Gubitchev must go on trial together next Tuesday.

And the sober-faced Gubitchev, who had refused up to now to enter any defense, changed his mind and decided to have a lawyer represent him.

Speaking in Russian, through an interpreter, Gubitchev said he hadn't thought there were good reasons to start a trial and had considered the case merely a "provocation."

"I think," he told Ryan, "it might be better for me to prepare my defense and take counsel."
